subtitle: Solving Ax = b two ways: a fixed number of steps (direct), or creeping closer each pass (iterative).

gauss.body:
Remember solving two equations by eliminating one unknown? You can do it for any number. Gaussian elimination does that for any number of equations, systematically. Write the system as an augmented matrix [A | b]. Forward elimination subtracts multiples of a pivot row to put zeros below the diagonal, giving an upper-triangular system; back-substitution then solves from the last unknown upward. The cost is ≈ n³/3 multiplications.

Try 2x + y − z = 8, −3x − y + 2z = −11, −2x + y + 2z = −3. Eliminate x from row 2 using row 1 with a multiplier m = −3/2: R₂ ← R₂ − mR₁. After the whole elimination, back-substitute: the last row gives z = −1, then y = 3, then x = 2. The solution is x, y, z = 2 3 -1. Why swap rows to use the largest available pivot? To avoid dividing by something tiny, which would magnify round-off errors.
keynotes: Gaussian elimination writes the system as [A | b], uses forward elimination to make it upper-triangular and back-substitution to solve from the last unknown upward; the cost is ≈ n³/3 multiplications.
For 2x + y − z = 8, −3x − y + 2z = −11, −2x + y + 2z = −3 the solution is x = 2, y = 3, z = −1.
Swapping rows to use the largest available pivot avoids dividing by something tiny.

sing.body:
Sometimes elimination hits a wall, and you should recognise it. If a zero pivot remains after pivoting, the matrix is singular: the system has no solution or infinitely many. Look: x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = 4 has infinitely many (the rows are dependent), while x + y = 2, x + y = 3 has none, since the two lines are parallel.

There is a gentler trouble too. Ill-conditioned systems (nearly singular) give wildly different answers for tiny changes in the data. That is a property of the problem, not the method. A zero pivot that cannot be removed by row swaps indicates a singular matrix.
keynotes: If a zero pivot remains after pivoting, the matrix is singular: the system has no solution or infinitely many.
x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = 4 has infinitely many solutions; x + y = 2, x + y = 3 has none.
Ill-conditioned (nearly singular) systems give wildly different answers for tiny changes in the data, a property of the problem, not the method.

iter.body:
For huge systems with mostly zeros, elimination is wasteful, as you will see. A cheaper idea: guess, then improve the guess again and again. Solve each equation for its own unknown: xᵢ = (bᵢ − Σⱼ≠ᵢ aᵢⱼxⱼ)/aᵢᵢ. Jacobi updates every unknown from the previous iterate; Gauss–Seidel uses each new value immediately, usually converging about twice as fast. In the figures, Jacobi uses all old values and Gauss–Seidel uses new values at once.

When does it work? Both converge if the matrix is diagonally dominant (|aᵢᵢ| > Σ|aᵢⱼ| on every row). For 10x − y + 2z = 6, −x + 11y − z = 25, 2x − y + 10z = −11 (dominant: yes) the answer is 1.04327 2.26923 -1.08173 after 12 Gauss–Seidel sweeps. Diagonal dominance guarantees convergence of both methods.
keynotes: Iterative methods solve each equation for its own unknown: xᵢ = (bᵢ − Σⱼ≠ᵢ aᵢⱼxⱼ)/aᵢᵢ.
Jacobi updates every unknown from the previous iterate; Gauss–Seidel uses each new value immediately and usually converges about twice as fast.
Both converge if the matrix is diagonally dominant; the example reaches 1.04327, 2.26923, −1.08173 after 12 Gauss–Seidel sweeps.

cmp.body:
Direct or iterative: which should you choose? Direct methods (elimination, LU) give an answer after a fixed amount of work and handle any non-singular matrix, but cost O(n³) and fill in zeros. Iterative methods cost O(n) per sweep for sparse matrices and can stop at the accuracy you need, but may not converge. Real solvers use LU for moderate sizes and preconditioned Krylov methods for huge sparse ones.

See the gap. A system with n = 10 000 unknowns and 5 non-zeros per row: one Gauss–Seidel sweep ≈ 5×10⁴ operations, while elimination ≈ n³/3 ≈ 3×10¹¹. Even 100 sweeps are far cheaper. For a huge sparse system an iterative method is attractive because each sweep is cheap.
keynotes: Direct methods (elimination, LU) give an answer after a fixed amount of work and handle any non-singular matrix, but cost O(n³) and fill in zeros.
Iterative methods cost O(n) per sweep for sparse matrices and can stop at the accuracy you need, but may not converge.
For n = 10 000 with 5 non-zeros per row, a sweep costs about 5×10⁴ operations against about 3×10¹¹ for elimination.

lu.body:
Suppose you must solve Ax = b for a hundred different b’s. Do you repeat the whole elimination a hundred times? No: you save the work. Gaussian elimination records its multipliers: A = LU with L lower-triangular (multipliers below a unit diagonal) and U the upper-triangular result. To solve Ax = b: solve Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back-substitution. Factor once, then solve for many right-hand sides cheaply.

Try A = [[2, 1], [4, 5]]. The multiplier m₂₁ = 4/2 = 2, so L = [[1, 0], [2, 1]]. Eliminate: row 2 − 2·row 1 gives [0, 3], so U = [[2, 1], [0, 3]]. The entries of L below the diagonal are exactly the multipliers used in elimination.
keynotes: Gaussian elimination records its multipliers: A = LU with L lower-triangular and U the upper-triangular result.
To solve Ax = b, solve Ly = b by forward substitution then Ux = y by back-substitution; factor once and solve for many right-hand sides cheaply.

summary.body:
Two lines to keep.

  • Elimination + pivoting is direct; Jacobi/Seidel iterate and need diagonal dominance.
  • LU reuses the work across right-hand sides.
keynotes: Elimination with pivoting is direct; Jacobi and Seidel iterate and need diagonal dominance.
LU reuses the work across right-hand sides.
